beats.label: ASSEMBLE

cue.prompt: Pick the tech that is genuinely part of you.

slides.text: Pick the tech that is genuinely part of you.
slides.note:
→ "Pick the tech that's genuinely part of you. Not what you own — what you'd feel the loss of."

→ "Glasses. Your keyboard layout. Your car. Your language. Your dialect."

slides.title: Seven axes, no endpoint
slides.note:
→ "This is a radar over seven axes, not a zero-to-a-hundred scale."

→ "Intimacy, dependence, agency, visibility, consent, mastery, surveillance."

→ "Every component you pick carries a score on all seven. Your shape is the average — so picking more things doesn't make you more cyborg, it changes your silhouette."

⚑ Say this explicitly. Grad students will notice if the instrument disagrees with the thesis, and the argument is sitting in the shape of the measurement.

beats.presenterNotes:
⏱ 3 min · no wrong answers, which is why this runs before any theory

· ASSEMBLE stays open the full forty minutes — tell them to revise as the argument moves. Revision is data.

beats.label: ETYMOLOGY

slides.text: For the exogenously extended organizational complex functioning as an integrated homeostatic system unconsciously, we propose the term 'Cyborg.'
slides.attrib: Manfred Clynes & Nathan Kline, "Cyborgs and Space," 1960
slides.note:
→ "Coined in 1960 by Manfred Clynes and Nathan Kline, in a paper called 'Cyborgs and Space.'"

→ "They were solving a concrete NASA problem: how do you keep a human body alive in an environment that wants to destroy it."

→ "Their proposal wasn't to build a massive Earth-like chamber. It was to modify the human — biologically and technologically — and integrate them directly into the mechanical loops of the vehicle."

→ "Read it word by word. 'Exogenously extended' — the extension is outside the skin. 'Homeostatic system' — self-regulating. And 'unconsciously.'"

→ "That last word is load-bearing. The whole definition turns on the system running below attention. If you notice your prosthesis constantly, integration has failed."

slides.text: They were describing space travel. I'm describing your phone.
slides.note: → "They were describing space travel. I'm describing your smartphone."

slides.text: The word began as an engineering requirement.
slides.note:
→ "The word began as an engineering requirement."

⏱ Let it sit, then move.

beats.presenterNotes: ⏱ 6 min · the word started as a spec, not a metaphor and not science fiction

beats.label: CYBERNETICS

cue.prompt: Where does your toolchain sit on this timeline?

slides.text: Feedback is the key. Feedback is the key to cybernetics, which is the key to the AI era.
slides.attrib: John Maeda, Design in Tech Report 2026, SXSW
slides.note:
→ "That's Maeda, at SXSW this year."

→ "Same underlying architecture across aircraft autopilot, car lane control, and coding-agent autoapprovals. The loop is the fundamental unit of an agentic system."

items: Closed loop — learning while you go
slides.note:
→ "Open loop means no feedback. Closed loop means learning while you're getting along."

→ "So if everything is feedback loops, interface design becomes conversation architecture. You're not designing screens — you're designing the terms of negotiation."

slides.text: Technology is anything we intentionally co-evolved.
slides.note:
→ "Technology is broad. Supercomputers and laptops, but also books, language and dialect."

→ "Cybernetics is the inflection point, because that's when technology starts talking back — and bidirectional influence becomes impossible to ignore."

→ "This is the DNA of McLuhan's argument. What's new is that the negotiation surface is now linguistic, which makes it obvious."

beats.presenterNotes:
⏱ 5 min · feedback → cybernetics → AI era

⏱ Student engagement, quick: "map your own tools onto this. Where does Figma sit? Where does a language model sit?" Take two answers from the feed, no more.

beats.label: RECOGNITION

cue.prompt: Where does technology stop and you begin?

slides.text: You don't need implants to be a cyborg.
slides.note:
→ "You don't need implants to be a cyborg."

→ "The normalcy of our daily interaction with technology makes genuinely immersive, technically complex moments feel mundane."

→ "Self-checkout kiosks. Autocorrect. Noise-cancelling headphones. GPS."

→ "This is the apparatus we're dressed in, and it's growing."

slides.text: Did you invent the words you are using? Did you design the glyphs?
slides.note:
→ "'That was written by AI' versus 'I wrote this by hand' is an awkward, unbalanced sentence."

→ "Did you invent the words? Did you design the glyphs? What constitutes authorship?"

items: Astronaut — body as system under constraint
You — with a model open in the next tab
slides.note:
→ "Vader's suit keeps him alive in a hostile environment. Conspicuous, self-directed, high mastery."

→ "The astronaut's suit does the same life-support job — but the astronaut is also managing the psychology of drinking recycled urine. The body as a system under constraint, and almost total consent gap. Life support as identity."

→ "The pilot is different again: the apparatus is trained reflex. High mastery, low surveillance."

→ "And the daily designer is the inversion of Vader. Invisible, dispatched, low mastery, high surveillance."

→ "Same argument, four silhouettes. None of them is further along than another."

→ "Imagine a world full of superheroes who don't realize they have the power. There's a simultaneous sadness and danger in a society of ultrapowerful beings not knowing their strength."

beats.presenterNotes:
⏱ 5 min · four different SHAPES, not four positions on a line

⚑ This is the beat where the old spectrum framing sneaks back in. Keep it about kind, not degree.

beats.label: AUTHENTICATION

cue.prompt: In your portfolio, how do you distinguish human from machine contribution? Should you?

slides.text: Language models destroyed the Turing test.
slides.note:
→ "Section 9 is obsessed with confirming identity in a world where identity can be forged, copied and transferred."

→ "That maps directly onto our moment: deepfakes, model impersonation, digital identity verification."

slides.text: The veil between I, we and technology is thinner than ever.
slides.note:
→ "If the Major questions the authenticity of her own memories — what does that say about models trained on human text? Are those responses memories, or fabricated experiences?"

→ "The GITS frame suggests that's the wrong question. When consciousness operates as technical process, the distinction between authentic and artificial memory collapses."

slides.text: Verification systems for fluid, distributed selves.
slides.note:
→ "Her uncertainty isn't a psychological crisis. It's a design specification."

→ "Section 9's authentication protocols break down because they assume a fixed identity. The design challenge is verification for fluid, constructable, distributed selves."

→ "Snow Crash is the cognitive limit case — the invisible terminal, where abstracted code rewrites our wet operating systems in an instant. Stephenson's parallel with the drug was no coincidence."

slides.text: How do you distinguish human from machine contribution in your own work? Should you?
slides.note:
→ "In your own portfolio work: how do you distinguish human from machine contribution? And should you?"

⏱ Take submissions on the feed.
· Stage two. Respond to the harder one first.

beats.presenterNotes: ⏱ 6 min · they'll push back hardest here — welcome it, model the uncertainty, don't defend the framework

beats.label: RESPONSIBILITY

cue.prompt: For whose interests does the interface serve?

slides.title: REGENT / THE SEAGLIDER
beats: Brief: an interface for a captain who can fly.
Then the test pilot showed up. Call sign: Bob Dylan.
"That's not where I expect it to be."
We weren't designing interface. We were translating fluency.
slides.note:
→ "Regent builds a ground-effect craft that skims above the water, hovering below FAA classification."

→ "The target operator was defined as a mariner. One wheel, one throttle — a captain that can fly. But the operational scope was aviation-grade and the mental model was maritime. That gap was the entire design problem."

→ "Then a test pilot joined. Ex-Air Force, F-16s in service, 747s commercially, tens of thousands of hours. Call sign a folksinger's name — we called him Bob Dylan."

→ "He liked every concept. Every concept was wrong — not because they were messy, but because they didn't match the logic his body had spent decades building."

→ "Pilots scan. They feel for what's off. They process feedback faster than conscious thought. His most common note was 'that's not where I expect it to be.'"

→ "I spent hours in Microsoft Flight Simulator learning how altimeters behave and where attitude indicators live. Every cockpit has a language, and I needed to be fluent enough to design in dialect."

→ "We ended with a recalibrated vocabulary, not a reinvented one. Semantic colour held to aviation standard — teal for set values, magenta for actuals."

→ "Here's the theoretical payload: negotiated agency. The user isn't just an actor — they're being acted upon. Systems push back. By design they suggest, limit, surveil, and even discipline."

→ "The experience isn't a smoothly-paved one-way street. It's a negotiation table."

slides.title: SELF-CHECKOUT
beats: The chain protecting margins. The card companies extracting fees.
Age verification. Municipal regulation. Produce indexing.
slides.note:
→ "Self-checkout makes the table visible."

→ "The grocery chain protecting margins. The card companies extracting fees. Age verification enforcing policy. Municipal regulations. Produce vendors dictating indexing. And the machine itself, ever-ready to flag 'unexpected item in the bagging area.'"

→ "To design responsibly in a cyborg world is to name these actors, question their power, and decide how — and whether — they belong at the table."

slides.text: Technological coevolution is not an even playing field.
slides.note: → "Technological coevolution is not an even playing field. It is always enacted on, and mediated by, a field of power."

slides.text: For whose interests does the interface serve?
slides.note: → "Go back to your pre-read interface. Whose interests does it serve? What negotiation table is it representing?"

beats.presenterNotes: ⏱ 7 min · longest beat — watch the clock

beats.label: STEWARD

cue.prompt: One sentence: what changes in your thesis if you frame it as assemblage integration?

slides.text: Cyborg describes what we are, not how we should be.
slides.note:
→ "Cyborg describes what we are, not how we should be. Diagnostic, not prescriptive."

⏱ Say this BEFORE the role list, so the roles read as options rather than instructions.

→ "Steward maintains, oversees. A curator is a professional arranger of stuff and context. Negotiator works the table."

→ "These aren't metaphors, they're job descriptions — roles to borrow from. 'User' fuses the person and the tool: what is a user without their apparatus?"

→ "Here's the distinction to leave with. Tool operation treats an external object manipulated by a separate person. Assemblage integration treats a component of an extended identity system."

→ "If you can see yourself as a cyborg, you understand your assemblage is part of you — which means you get to choose, like with clothing, how you build from and extend yourself."

→ "You should feel compelled to arrange it how you want. And frustrated when you can't control it. You probably already do."
